titulo_es: Reflexive pronouns (myself, themselves) and reciprocal pronouns (each other)
descripcion_es: When reflexive pronouns are used in English, the emphatic use and the difference from each other.
resumen: Reflexive pronouns (myself, yourself…) are used when the subject and the object are the same person, or for emphasis. Many Spanish pronominal verbs (with “se”) are NOT reflexive in English.

items: Sujeto y objeto coinciden: She cut herself. Enjoy yourselves!
Emphasis, “I did it personally”: I painted the house myself.
by + reflexive = alone, without help or without company: He lives by himself.
Useful expressions: help yourself (take what you want), behave yourself (be good), make yourself at home (feel at home).

explicacion.texto: Many verbs that take “se” in Spanish are not reflexive in English: get up (levantarse), wash (lavarse), shave (afeitarse), dress / get dressed (vestirse), relax (relajarse), feel (sentirse), remember (acordarse), meet (verse, quedar). You say I get up at seven, not I get myself up.
Each other (or one another) is reciprocal: They love each other = each one loves the other. They love themselves = each one loves himself or herself. In Spanish both are “se quieren”.

ejemplos.frase: Be careful with that knife or you'll hurt yourself.
ejemplos.traduccion: Ten cuidado con ese cuchillo o te harás daño.

ejemplos.frase: She travelled around Asia by herself.
Ana and Luis call each other every evening.
ejemplos.traduccion: Ana y Luis se llaman todas las noches.

ejemplos.frase: Please help yourselves to some cake.
I usually get up early and shower before breakfast.
ejemplos.traduccion: Suelo levantarme temprano y ducharme antes de desayunar.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: I wake myself up at seven every day.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: I wake up at seven every day.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: Wake up is not reflexive in English even though Spanish “despertarse” is.

errores_hispanohablantes.bien: They looked at each other and smiled.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: If the action is mutual (they looked at one another), you use each other.
Feel does not take a reflexive: Spanish “me siento cansado” = I feel tired.

ejercicios.frase: Did you enjoy ___ at the party, girls?
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the table on the card: for plural you the reflexive is yourselves. The clue is girls, which shows you are speaking to several people. Enjoy needs an object when it means “have a good time”, and since the people having a good time are the subject themselves, the reflexive is used: enjoy yourselves.
ejercicios.traduccion: ¿Os lo pasasteis bien en la fiesta, chicas?

errores_previstos.explicacion: Yourself is singular; girls shows plural: yourselves.
The plural of self is selves: yourselves.
The subject and the object are the same people, so you need the reflexive: yourselves.

ejercicios.frase: The cat was cleaning ___ in the sun.
ejercicios.explicacion: The rule on the card is to use the reflexive when the subject acts on itself: the cat washes itself. For an animal referred to as it, the reflexive is itself. The card also accepts herself or himself if it is a pet whose sex is known, because in English it is common to refer to pets like this.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Animal referred to as it: itself (for a pet whose sex is known, herself/himself is also fine).
ejercicios.traduccion: El gato se estaba lavando al sol.

errores_previstos.explicacion: The subject and the object are the same: you need the reflexive itself.
Its is a possessive; the reflexive is itself.
There is only one cat: itself, in the singular.

ejercicios.frase: He taught ___ to play the guitar.
ejercicios.explicacion: The card explains the reflexive use: when the subject and the object are the same person. Teach someone to do something means showing someone how to do something; if you teach yourself, the object is the reflexive. With he you use himself. Teach himself means “learn on his own”.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Subject he: himself (he learnt on his own).
ejercicios.traduccion: Aprendió solo a tocar la guitarra.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Him would mean he taught another person; if he learnt on his own, it is himself.
Hisself does not exist in standard English: the form is himself.
The subject is he: himself.

ejercicios.frase: We don't need help. We can do it ___.
ejercicios.explicacion: This is the emphatic use on the card: the reflexive stresses that the subject does it personally, without help. The clue is We don't need help. With we the reflexive is ourselves, which goes at the end of the sentence, after the object it.
ejercicios.traduccion: No necesitamos ayuda. Podemos hacerlo nosotros mismos.

errores_previstos.explicacion: With we the reflexive is plural: ourselves.
Us is an object pronoun; to say “we did it personally” you use the reflexive ourselves.
The plural of self is selves: ourselves.

ejercicios.frase: My grandmother lives by ___ in a small flat.
ejercicios.explicacion: The card explains that by + reflexive means “alone, without company”. The clue is the preposition by before the gap. My grandmother is she, so the reflexive is herself: by herself. You could also say alone, with the same meaning.
ejercicios.traduccion: Mi abuela vive sola en un piso pequeño.

errores_previstos.explicacion: By her would mean “next to her”; for “alone” you use by herself.
The grandmother is she: herself.
By alone does not exist; either lives alone or lives by herself.

ejercicios.frase: Marta and Elena have known ___ since primary school.
ejercicios.explicacion: The card distinguishes each other (reciprocal: one knows the other) from themselves (each one knows herself). In Spanish both are “se conocen”, hence the confusion. Here the relationship is mutual: Marta knows Elena and Elena knows Marta, so it is each other.
ejercicios.traduccion: Marta y Elena se conocen desde primaria.

por_opcion.themselves: It would mean each of them knows herself, not that they know each other.
por_opcion.each other: Correct: it expresses the mutual relationship between Marta and Elena.
por_opcion.theirselves: It does not exist in standard English; the plural reflexive is themselves.

ejercicios.frase: I usually ___ at 7.30 and have a quick breakfast.
ejercicios.explicacion: The card warns that many verbs that take “se” in Spanish are not reflexive in English, and Spanish “vestirse” is one of them: get dressed. No pronoun is added. Dress up means something else: to put on a costume or to dress smartly for a special occasion.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Putting your clothes on (es: vestirse) is normally get dressed, with no reflexive.
ejercicios.traduccion: Normalmente me visto a las 7.30 y desayuno algo rápido.

por_opcion.get dressed: Correct: it is the normal way to say you put your clothes on.
por_opcion.dress myself up: Dress up means “put on a costume” or “dress smartly”; besides, the reflexive is unnecessary in a normal routine.
por_opcion.get me dressed: Get me dressed would mean another person dresses me; for yourself it is get dressed.

ejercicios.frase: Come in and make ___ at home.
ejercicios.explicacion: Make yourself at home is one of the fixed expressions on the card and means “feel at home, be comfortable”. It is a reflexive use: the implicit subject of the imperative is you, so it is yourself. It cannot be replaced by you or by your.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Fixed expression: make yourself at home.
ejercicios.traduccion: Pasa y estás en tu casa.

por_opcion.you: Make you at home is ungrammatical; the fixed expression takes the reflexive yourself.
por_opcion.yourself: Correct: fixed expression make yourself at home.
por_opcion.your: Your is a possessive and needs a noun after it.

ejercicios.frase: Don't worry about me. I can look after ___.
ejercicios.explicacion: The rule on the card says you use the reflexive when the subject and the object are the same person. Look after means “take care of”; if I take care of myself, the object is myself. Me would be wrong because the subject is already I.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: The subject and the object are the same person: myself.
ejercicios.traduccion: No te preocupes por mí. Sé cuidarme solo.

por_opcion.me: With the subject I, an object referring to the same person must be reflexive: myself.
por_opcion.myself: Correct: the subject and the object are the same.
por_opcion.each other: Each other expresses a mutual action between several people; here there is only one.

ejercicios.frase: I need to relax myself after work.
respuestas: I need to relax after work.
ejercicios.explicacion: The card includes relax among the verbs that take “se” in Spanish but are not reflexive in English. Relax alone is enough, with no pronoun. Adding myself is a calque of Spanish “relajarme” and sounds forced.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Relax is not used with a reflexive in English.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I need to relax myself after work.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the uncorrected sentence: relax does not take a reflexive.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I need to relax me after work.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Calque of Spanish “relajarme”: relax does not take a pronoun.
The reflexive has been removed, but need needs to before the verb: need to relax.

ejercicios.frase: They did all the work theirselves.
respuestas: They did all the work themselves.
ejercicios.explicacion: This is the emphatic use on the card (“they did it personally”). The correct plural reflexive is themselves; theirselves is heard in some informal varieties, but it is not standard English. The rule is easy to remember: myself, yourself, ourselves use the possessive, but himself and themselves use the object pronoun.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: The correct form is themselves; theirselves does not exist in standard English.
ejercicios.traduccion: Hicieron todo el trabajo ellos mismos.

errores_previstos.respuesta: They did all the work theirselves.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the uncorrected sentence: theirselves is not standard.

errores_previstos.respuesta: They did all the work themself.
errores_previstos.explicacion: With plural they the standard form is themselves.

errores_previstos.respuesta: They did all the work each other.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Each other expresses a mutual action; here the emphasis “they did it personally” is needed.

ejercicios.frase: We met ourselves at the station at nine.
respuestas: We met at the station at nine.
We met each other at the station at nine.
ejercicios.explicacion: The card gives meet as the translation of Spanish “quedar” or “verse”, and makes clear that it takes no reflexive. We met at the station is enough. You can add each other, which the card accepts, because the action is mutual; but ourselves would mean we met ourselves, which makes no sense.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Spanish “quedar/verse” is meet, with no reflexive.
ejercicios.traduccion: Quedamos en la estación a las nueve.

errores_previstos.respuesta: We met ourselves at the station at nine.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the uncorrected sentence: meet does not take a reflexive.

errores_previstos.respuesta: We met us at the station at nine.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Calque of Spanish “nos vimos”: meet does not need a pronoun.

errores_previstos.respuesta: We stayed at the station at nine.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Stay means “remain in a place”, not “arrange to see someone” (es: quedar con alguien): meet.

respuestas: please help yourself to the food
help yourself to the food please
ejercicios.explicacion: The card includes help yourself as a fixed expression (“take what you want”). What you take is introduced with the preposition to: help yourself to the food. Please can go at the beginning or at the end. A calque of Spanish (“sírvete”) would lead you to leave out to or to use serve, which is not used like this in English.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Help yourself to + something = take what you want of it.
ejercicios.traduccion: Por favor, sírvete la comida. (También: Sírvete la comida, por favor.)

errores_previstos.respuesta: please help the food to yourself
errores_previstos.explicacion: The reflexive goes right after help, and what you take goes after to: help yourself to the food.

errores_previstos.respuesta: please yourself help to the food
errores_previstos.explicacion: Yourself goes after the verb help, not before it.

ejercicios.explicacion: The card explains that each other expresses a mutual action: each one hates the other. It goes after the verb like a normal object: They hate each other. In Spanish “se odian” could be reciprocal or reflexive; in English you have to choose, and here with each other the meaning is reciprocal.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Each other for a mutual action.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Calque of the Spanish order (“se odian”): each other goes after the verb.
Each other works as an object and goes after the verb.

descripcion_larga_es: Reflexive pronouns (myself, yourself, themselves…) are used when the subject and the object are the same person and for emphasis (“I did it personally”). The big trap for Spanish speakers is that many verbs with “se” in Spanish are not reflexive in English: levantarse, relajarse, vestirse or quedar are get up, relax, get dressed or meet. Also, Spanish “se quieren” can be themselves or each other.

contexto.que_es: These are pronouns ending in -self (singular) or -selves (plural) that refer back to the subject of the same sentence. They have three uses: reflexive (the action falls on the subject), emphatic (personally, without help) and, with by, the meaning “alone”.
contexto.por_que_importa: Using them correctly avoids one of the most frequent calques from Spanish: adding a reflexive to verbs that do not take one in English (I relax myself, we met ourselves), which sounds strange and sometimes changes the meaning. Distinguishing themselves from each other is necessary so as not to say something different from what you mean. Expressions such as help yourself or make yourself at home are common in social life.
contexto.cuando_se_usa: When the subject acts on itself (hurt yourself, enjoy yourselves), to stress that someone did something personally (I painted it myself) and with by for “alone” (by herself). It is not used with get up, wash, shave, relax, feel, remember or meet in their normal use. For mutual actions (Spanish “se conocen”, “se odian”) you use each other.
